legacy_report:
SOURCE: Composer 2 Technical Report, Cursor Research Team (Rush, Muennighoff, Truell, Sanger and others, Appendix A), arXiv 2603.24477v2 [cs.SE], 26 Mar 2026. Preprint.

COVERAGE: 75,469 of 75,469 chars, all 23 pages. I read the body (pp. 1-14), appendices B and C (pp. 21-23) and the contributor list. I only skimmed the reference list (pp. 14-21), for origins. The extraction is clean. Figure plots are images, so I could not read their values; I read captions only.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Composer 2 scores 61.3 on CursorBench-3, 73.7 on SWE-bench Multilingual and 61.7 on Terminal-Bench, all in Cursor's own harness. Composer 1.5 gets 44.2/65.9/47.9 and Composer 1 gets 38.0/56.9/40.0.
  number: 61.3 / 73.7 / 61.7
  setup: Composer models are scored in Cursor's harness. Third-party models are listed as (our harness / self-reported). Anthropic models on Terminal-Bench use Claude Code leaderboard scores. Opus 4.6 High scores 58.2 on CursorBench, GPT-5.4 63.9, GPT-5.3 Codex 59.1, Kimi K2.5 36.0. Refused GPT problems are scored as 0.
  quote: "Composer 2 achieves 61.3%, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 and a 61% improvement over Composer 1."
  where: Table 1 and §7.1, pp. 13-14
- claim: The base model is Kimi K2.5. Composer 2 improves a lot over it on CursorBench (61.3 vs 36.0) and Terminal-Bench (61.7 vs 47.3). On SWE-bench Multilingual it is similar (73.7 vs 65.1 in Cursor's harness, 73.0 self-reported). The authors attribute the gain to continued pretraining plus RL. No ablation separates the two stages.
  number: 61.3 vs 36.0 on CursorBench
  setup: Kimi K2.5 is a 1.04T-parameter, 32B-active MoE.
  quote: "Compared to its base model, Kimi K2.5, Composer 2 demonstrates a substantial accuracy boost, validating the effectiveness of our continued pretraining and reinforcement learning pipeline."
  where: §7.1, p. 13
- claim: RL did not trade average performance for best-of-K. Both rose together, which the authors read as RL widening effective coverage rather than only reweighting known paths.
  number: none (Figure 5 curves only)
  setup: Held-out eval set plus CursorBench tasks. Values not extractable.
  quote: "rather than observing a trade-off in which average reward rises while best-of-K remains flat, we find that our training improves both statistics as shown in Figure 5."
  where: §4.1, p. 5
- claim: RL algorithm. Policy gradient with a fixed group size, single epoch (no prompt is reused), full-parameter Adam. It follows Dr. GRPO, so there is no length normalisation and no division by the group standard deviation. Overlong rollouts are not masked. KL uses the k1 estimator, not k3, because k3 variance explodes when p and q diverge.
  number: none
  setup: Reasons given are length bias, degenerate upweighting when all rollouts are equally correct, and k3 variance blow-up at large KL. The no-masking choice is based on "small scale" tests and the self-summary system.
  quote: "We do not normalize group advantages by their standard deviation, as it results in the degenerate case where small behavioral differences get massively upweighted within a group where every rollout achieves equal correctness."
  where: §4.1, p. 4
- claim: Asynchronous RL stability comes from keeping samples close to on-policy. The methods are fast weight sync, in-flight weight updates mid-rollout (like PipelineRL), and MoE router replay. Replay is extended by filtering out replayed experts whose gating scores fall below a plausibility threshold, which cuts p99 numerics mismatch.
  number: none
  setup: Inference runs on Fireworks AI. Weights sync each step as delta-compressed diffs through S3, and the diffs compress to "a handful of gigabytes" for the 1T model.
  quote: "Inference workers are capable of updating weights mid-rollout, which means later tokens in a rollout are likely less off-policy. To reduce further divergence between the sampling and training policy, we replay MoE routing"
  where: §4.1 p. 4, §6.2 pp. 11-12
- claim: Self-summarization is trained end to end. A rollout is several generations chained by summaries. The final reward is applied to every token, including the summary tokens, so good summaries are upweighted and lossy ones downweighted. It beats separate prompt-based compaction and reuses the KV cache.
  number: none (no figure given)
  setup: The technique was introduced in Composer 1.5. The paper gives no number for the error reduction.
  quote: "we find that self-summary consistently reduces the error compared to using separate prompt-based compaction, while using significantly fewer tokens and reusing the KV cache."
  where: §4.1, p. 5
- claim: Train-test match is the core principle. RL runs in the same Cursor harness as production, with the same tools. Tools come from a shadow deployment of the Cursor backend and are called over RPC. The task distribution is real coding-session categories (Figure 3). Tool sets and strictness can differ per environment, for example stricter argument checks and removed tools. Rollouts run in Firecracker VMs on the internal Anyrun platform.
  number: ">500 pods per second" per Anyrun cluster, hundreds of thousands of pods per cluster
  setup: Anyrun supports filesystem and memory snapshots and forking. This enables rollout checkpointing, and recovery passes the reconstructed environment to verifiers. Egress goes through the Anygress proxy. The training job spanned 3 GPU regions and 4 CPU regions.
  quote: "A core tenet of Composer training is to emulate real-world user challenges as closely as possible to minimize train-test mismatch."
  where: §1 p. 1, §6.2 pp. 10-11
- claim: Behaviour shaping uses auxiliary rewards (coding style, communication, penalties for poor tool use such as unfinished to-do items). The team also adds rewards for emergent bad behaviours when they appear. A concave-down, increasing length penalty makes the model quick on easy tasks and lets it think longer on hard ones. It also taught efficient behaviour such as parallel tool calls.
  number: C_length{k,q}(x) = ((1+kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q))
  setup: The input x is a weighted mix of thinking tokens, tool-call tokens, tool-output tokens, final-message tokens, number of tool calls and number of turns. k and q are hyperparameters. Their values are not given.
  quote: "we observed that the model would start to leave long chains-of-thought in comments or collapse to using the terminal tool only."
  where: §4.2, pp. 5-6
- claim: Continued pretraining loss predicts downstream RL reward. Final post-SFT loss was compared against RL reward at a fixed step count across three compute levels.
  number: "three logarithmically spaced compute levels"
  setup: Done on Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, not on Kimi. Each checkpoint got small-dataset SFT and then an identical RL run. Only three points, read from Figure 2 left. Codebase loss falls log-linearly on the main run.
  quote: "demonstrating that cross-entropy loss is indeed predictive of downstream RL performance."
  where: §3.1, p. 3
- claim: Continued pretraining recipe. Three phases: most compute at 32k sequence length, then long-context extension to 256k, then a short SFT on targeted coding tasks. Trained in MXFP8 on B300s with AdamW. Multi-Token Prediction layers are trained by self-distillation for speculative decoding.
  number: 32k then 256k
  setup: MTP layers are initialised from scratch and trained on a mid-run checkpoint.
  quote: "We spend the bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length, followed by a shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks."
  where: §3.1, p. 2
- claim: Numerics matter for RL stability. The MoE forward pass uses a custom NVFP4 variant with FP32 per-token scales instead of per-tensor scales. The backward pass uses MXFP8. Fast-approximation division in NVFP4 quantization diverges.
  number: "after roughly a hundred RL steps"
  setup: Per-tensor scaling makes training batch-variant and leaks future-token information into past tokens through the scales. The trainer forward pass must match inference, but the backward pass can use higher precision because it runs only on the training cluster.
  quote: "using fast-approximation alternatives causes training to diverge after roughly a hundred RL steps."
  where: §6.1, p. 10
- claim: Cost-accuracy trade-off. Composer 2 is on the Pareto frontier of median inference cost per CursorBench task, with token usage comparable to other frontier models.
  number: none (Figure 11 plot only)
  setup: Cost is compared with GPT-5.4, Codex-5.3, Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 at high, medium and low effort. API price is used because FLOPs are not available.
  quote: "its inference cost is similar to smaller or low-effort variants of models, while its accuracy remains competitive with much larger frontier models."
  where: §7.1, p. 13
- claim: CursorBench has less-specified prompts and larger edits than public benchmarks. The authors argue public benchmarks are contaminated and over-specified.
  number: median 181 lines changed vs 7-10 for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Median prompt 390 chars vs 1,185-3,055.
  setup: Internal tasks come from the team's own sessions. CursorBench-3 changes more than twice as many files and lines as the first version. Haiku 4.5 at 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified is close to GPT-5.4 at 74.9%, which the authors cite as compressed differences.
  quote: "a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7–10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual"
  where: §5, p. 7
- claim: Base-model selection used FreshBench (coding knowledge), state tracking and codebase perplexity, not agent benchmarks. Kimi K2.5 was chosen. It scored below DeepSeek V3.2 on perplexity and state tracking, so efficiency in Cursor's infrastructure also counted.
  number: Kimi K2.5 83.2% FreshBench, state tracking 86, NLL 13.81M. DeepSeek V3.2 68.9%, 66, 11.75M. GLM-5 79.2%, 92, 14.11M.
  setup: State tracking is average character distance, lower is better. NLL is measured on a private monorepo.
  quote: "We intentionally do not consider coding agent benchmarks when testing base models. We find that such benchmarks are less predictive of final performance, as agentic and long-horizon capabilities can drastically change during the RL stage."
  where: Appendix B, pp. 21-22
- claim: Training data difficulty is upsampled in later stages using simple heuristics.
  number: none
  setup: Heuristics are the number of turns and the thinking tokens of rollouts.
  quote: "we use simple heuristics—such as number of turns and thinking tokens of rollouts—to upsample increasingly harder data points."
  where: §4, p. 4

LIMITS
- The paper reports no ablations. It gives no training curves with values for the algorithm choices (no std-normalisation, k1 KL, no overlong masking, length penalty). It gives no reward-function details beyond the description above: correctness, succinctness and conformance to engineering principles, plus the auxiliary rewards. It gives no RL compute, steps or group size.
- CursorBench is internal and not released. The "our harness" numbers are Cursor's own, and the headline gap to others is a few points, with GPT-5.4 higher on CursorBench (63.9). Third-party runs had refusals scored as 0.
- The pretraining-loss to RL-reward link is shown on a different, smaller model (Qwen) with three compute points. The paper itself calls the link "an area of active research".
- The best-of-K claim is shown only as curves, with no numbers and no comparison against a baseline RL recipe.
- The authors concede that "there are many cases where the model shows intelligence or coherence behaviors that can be clearly improved". They say the model is "likely smaller than other proprietary models of comparative ability", and future work is longer horizons and better long-term training signal.
- The paper credits no per-component gain to continued pretraining versus RL.
- Dated: the model names and benchmark scores are valid as of March 2026.

BUILDS ON
- GRPO-style multi-sample policy gradients: Shao et al. [53] and Ahmadian et al. 2024 (REINFORCE-style [2]).
- Dr. GRPO, Liu et al. [34], for the unbiased advantage.
- DAPO-style overlong masking, Yu et al. [78], with Du et al. [13] and Golubev et al. [18] cited in the discussion.
- KL estimators: Schulman [52] for k3, Amini et al. NeurIPS 2025 [6] for the variance critique.
- PipelineRL [48] for in-flight weight updates.
- MoE router replay [38] and [82].
- Self-summarization from Composer 1.5 [64].
- Continued pretraining: Gururangan et al. 2020 [20].
- Multi-token prediction: Gloeckle et al. 2024 [17] and DeepSeek-V3 [11].
- Context parallelism: Liu et al. [33].
- RL-narrowing literature: [79, 32, 8, 74, 61].
- Base models: Kimi K2.5 [67], Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B [68].
- Infrastructure: Ray [42], PyTorch [47], DeepEP [80], ThunderKittens [56, 59], FlashAttention 4 with Colfax.
- Benchmarks: LoCoDiff [3], SWE-bench Multilingual [28], Terminal-Bench [39].

CODE
- Length penalty (§4.2, p. 5), as extracted: "Clength{k,q} (x) = (1+kx) 1−q −1k(1−q)", i.e. C(x) = ((1+kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)).
- KL estimator (§4.1, p. 4): "KL(q∥p) = Ex∼q [−logr(x) ], r(x) = p(x)/q(x)", and "k3 = (r−1)−logr", with k1 = −log r the one used.
- Appendix C.1 (pp. 22-23) has a Python reference diff for detecting growing-prefix streaming chains (find_prefix_chain, MIN_CHAIN=3). It is a benchmark-task example, not a training method, and not worth keeping.

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p. 3): continued-pretraining loss against RL reward on Qwen3-Coder-30B (left), and training perplexity falling on the main run (right).
- Fig 3 (p. 3): bar chart of the RL task category mix. Iterate-on-feature, Debugging and New Feature are the top categories.
- Fig 4 (p. 4): k1/k2/k3 KL estimator variance on synthetic Gaussians. It shows the k3 blow-up quickly.
- Fig 5 (p. 5): average and best-of-K both rise during RL. It is the key evidence for the "no diversity collapse" claim.
- Fig 6 (p. 5): the nonlinear length-penalty curves.
- Fig 7 (p. 6): CursorBench against public benchmarks on lines changed and prompt length.
- Fig 9 (p. 8): growth of CursorBench across versions.
- Fig 11 (p. 12): cost and token efficiency Pareto plot against frontier models at each effort level.
- Figs 1, 8, 10 and 12 are the headline bar chart, the example tasks and a kernel diagram, so less useful for the note.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found. The PDF text sits in /tmp/c2.txt (extraction copy, not a report).
- Figure values (Figures 2, 5, 6, 11) are not recoverable from text. Use the captions and the stated claims only.
- The extraction garbles the formula spacing, and the code listing in Appendix C is spaced oddly.
